newsitem.title: USA: Conn. physicians urge managed care reform.
newsitem.headline: Conn. physicians urge managed care reform.

text.p: Connecticut physicians, consumer groups and selected lawmakers on Tuesday urged the state to follow New Jersey's example in enacting sweeping reforms to managed health care.

"It is only appropriate that the state known as the insurance capital of the world should take a leadership role in oversight of this industry," Republican state Representative Lenny Winkler told a news conference.
The coalition said major reforms were needed to protect patients' rights and ensure adequate oversight of the system.
They said Connecticut is one of the few states in the country with no legal regulations to ensure that health plan members understand their coverage and get the care they are entitled to.

"Another reason that has people clamoring for reform is that the for-profit, managed care industry has an indisputable fiduciary responsibility to maximize profits for its shareholders," said Timothy Norbeck, executive director of the Connecticut State Medical Society.

He said that while shareholders have every right to expect profits, "How can we be certain, short of regulation, that fiduciary responsibility will not place 'cost effective' care considerations ahead of needed and compassionate care?"
Rather than supporting a specific bill, the participants in the news conference said they agreed on the kinds of general reforms needed. These included:
-Establishing independent medical oversight of the standards used by managed care organizations to make coverage decisions.
-Establishing an independent appeal mechanism for patients.
-Requiring managed care plans to clearly disclose a wide range of information, including coverage provisions.
-Prohibiting "gag rules" that prevent health care providers from communicating openly with their patients.
-Requiring that hospital admission and discharge decisions be made by the physician directly caring for the patient.
They said it is imperative that state lawmakers approve the reforms during the current legislative session which ends in June.
The sweeping reforms in New Jersey will take effect over a four-month period starting March 15.

Among other things, the New Jersey regulations will give two million consumers the right to appeal a health maintenance organization (HMO)'s decision to deny or limit care, allow only doctors to limit care, and require HMOs to undergo regular performance reviews.
Managed care is defined as a system that aims to control costs partly by controlling a patient's access to medical services, often by the use of a gatekeeper.
